questions.q: A uniform rod $AB$ of mass $2kg$ and Length $30cm$ at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. An impulse of force $0 . 2Ns$ is applied to end B. The time taken by the rod to turn through at right angles will be $\dfrac{\pi}{x}s,$ where $x =$ ____.
questions.solution:
Impulse $J = 0 . 2Ns$

$⇒ J = ∫ Fdt = 0 . 2Ns$

Now, angular impulse $( \overset{\to}{M} )$ will be

${M}_{c} = ∫ τdt$

$= ∫ F\dfrac{L}{2}dt$

$= \dfrac{L}{2} ∫ Fdt = \dfrac{L}{2} \times J$

$= \dfrac{0 . 3}{2} \times 0 . 2$

$= 0 . 03$

Moment of inertia of the rod about the centre of mass, ${I}_{cm} = \dfrac{M{L}^{2}}{12} = \dfrac{2 \times ( 0 . 3{)}^{2}}{12} = \dfrac{0 . 09}{6}$

Angular impulse will be equal to the change in angular momentum.

$M = {I}_{cm}\left({\omega}_{f} - {\omega}_{i}\right)$

$⇒ 0 . 03 = \dfrac{0 . 09}{6}\left({\omega}_{f}\right)$

$⇒ {\omega}_{f} = 2rad{s}^{- 1}$

For angular displacement, we can write $\theta = \omegat$

$⇒ t = \dfrac{\theta}{\omega} = \dfrac{\pi}{2 \times 2} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}s$.

Therefore, $x = 4$.

questions.q: A spherical body of mass $100g$ is dropped from a height of $10m$ from the ground. After hitting the ground, the body rebounds to a height of $5m$. The impulse of force imparted by the ground to the body is given by: (given $g = 9 . 8m{s}^{- 2}$)
questions.solution:
Using equation of motion with constant acceleration, we can write:

${v}_{1} = \sqrt{2g{h}_{1}}$ and ${v}_{2} = \sqrt{2g{h}_{2}}$

Now, required impulse

$\overset{\to}{I} = \Delta\overset{\to}{p} = \overset{\to}{p}f - \overset{\to}{p}i$

Given, $M = 0 . 1kg$

Therefore,

$I = \Deltap = 0 . 1 ( \sqrt{2 \times 9 . 8 \times 5} - ( - \sqrt{2 \times 9 . 8 \times 10} ) )$

$= 0 . 1 ( 7\sqrt{2} + 14 ) \approx 2 . 39kgm{s}^{- 1}$

questions.q: At what distance above and below the surface of the earth a body will have same weight? (Take radius of earth as $R$)
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the Earth is given by

${g}_{p} = \dfrac{g{R}^{2}}{( R + h{)}^{2}} . . . \left(1\right)$

The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $h$ below the surface of the Earth is given by

${g}_{q} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{R}\right) . . . \left(2\right)$

According to the given problem,

${g}_{p} = {g}_{q} . . . \left(3\right)$

Equations (1), (2) and (3) imply that

$\dfrac{g}{{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)}^{2}} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{R}\right) ⇒ \left(1 - \dfrac{{h}^{2}}{{R}^{2}}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right) = 1 . . . \left(4\right)$

Take $\dfrac{h}{R} = x$

So, from equation (4), it follows that

${x}^{3} - x + {x}^{2} = 0 ⇒ {x}^{2} + x - 1 = 0 ⇒ x = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} ⇒ h = \dfrac{R}{2} ( \sqrt{5} - 1 )$

questions.q: Four identical particles of mass $m$ are kept at the four corners of a square. If the gravitational force exerted on one of the masses by the other masses is $\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{32}\right)\dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{L}^{2}}$, the length of the sides of the square is

Resultant force, ${F}_{net} = \sqrt{2}F + F '$, where

$F = \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}$ and $F ' = \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{\left(\sqrt{2}a\right)}^{2}}$

Therefore, ${F}_{net} = \sqrt{2}\dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{2{a}^{2}}$

Comparing with the expression given in the question, we get

$\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{32}\right)\dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{L}^{2}} = \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{2}\right)$

$⇒ a = 4L$

Assertion (A) : The angular speed of the moon in its orbit about the earth is more than the angular speed of the earth in its orbit about the sun.
Reason (R): The moon takes less time to move around the earth than the time taken by the earth to move around the sun.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct
Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of A.
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of A.
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
It is known that

$\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} ⇒ \omega ∝ \dfrac{1}{T}$

As,
${T}_{\text{moon}} \approx 27$ days
${T}_{\text{earth}} \approx 365$ days
$⇒ {\omega}_{\text{moon}} > {\omega}_{\text{earth}}$

Hence, Both the assertion and the reason are correct and the reason is the correct explanation for the assertion.

questions.q: The relation between time ‘$t$’ and distance ‘$x$’ is $t = \alpha{x}^{2} + \betax$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants. The relation between acceleration $\left(a\right)$ and velocity $\left(v\right)$ is:
questions.solution:
Given: $t = \alpha{x}^{2} + \betax$ 

Differentiating w.r.t time, we get

$\dfrac{dt}{dx} = 2\alphax + \beta$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{v} = 2\alphax + \beta$

Differentiating w.r.t time again, we get

$⇒ - \dfrac{1}{{v}^{2}}\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 2\alpha\dfrac{dx}{dt}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dv}{dt} = - 2\alpha{v}^{3}\left[\text{as}v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}\right] ⇒ a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = - 2\alpha{v}^{3}$

If the $x$-coordinate of the particle at that instant is $84m$, then the speed of the particle at this time is $\sqrt{\alpha}m{s}^{- 1}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
questions.solution:
Given, ${u}_{x} = 5m{s}^{- 1}, {a}_{x} = 3m{s}^{- 2}, x = 84m$

The formula to calculate the velocity of the particle along x-axis is given by

${v}_{x}^{2} = {u}_{x}^{2} + 2ax . . . \left(1\right)$

From equation (1), it follows that

${v}_{x}^{2} = 25 + 2 ( 3 ) ( 84 ) ⇒ {v}_{x} = 23m{s}^{- 1}$

Also, the velocity of the particle along x-axis can be written as

${v}_{x} = {u}_{x} + {a}_{x}t . . . \left(2\right)$

From equation (2), it follows that

$\begin{cases}t & = & \dfrac{23 - 5}{3} \\ & = & 6s\end{cases}$

Similarly, for the $y -$ component of the velocity, it follows that

$\begin{cases}{v}_{y} & = & 0 + {a}_{y}t \\ & = & 0 + 2 \times ( 6 ) \\ & = & 12m{s}^{- 1}\end{cases}$

Hence, the magnitude of the velocity is given by

${v}^{2} = {v}_{x}^{2} + {v}_{y}^{2} = {23}^{2} + {12}^{2} = 673v = \sqrt{673}m{s}^{- 1}$

Therefore, $\alpha = 673$.

questions.q: A bullet is fired into a fixed target looses one third of its velocity after travelling $4cm$. It penetrates further $D \times {10}^{- 3}m$ before coming to rest. The value of $D$ is :
questions.solution:
When the bullet just enters the target, its equation of motion is given by

${v}^{2} - {u}^{2} = 2aS . . . \left(1\right)$

Equation (1) implies that

${\left(\dfrac{2u}{3}\right)}^{2} = {u}^{2} + 2\left(- a\right)\left(4 \times {10}^{- 2}\right) ⇒ \dfrac{4{u}^{2}}{9} = {u}^{2} - 2a\left(4 \times {10}^{- 2}\right) ⇒ \dfrac{5{u}^{2}}{9} = 2a\left(4 \times {10}^{- 2}\right) \ldots \left(2\right)$

When the bullet stops inside the target, its equation of motion can be written as

$0 = {\left(\dfrac{2u}{3}\right)}^{2} + 2\left(- a\right)\left(x\right) . . . \left(3\right)$

Equation (3) implies that

$\dfrac{4{u}^{2}}{9} = 2ax . . . \left(4\right)$

Dividing equation (2) by equation (4), we have

$\dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{4 \times {10}^{- 2}}{x} ⇒ x = \dfrac{16}{5} \times {10}^{- 2} ⇒ x = 3 . 2 \times {10}^{- 2}m = 32 \times {10}^{- 3}m$

Hence, $D = 32$.

questions.q: If a rubber ball falls from a height $h$ and rebounds upto the height of $h / 2$. The percentage loss of total energy of the initial system as well as velocity ball before it strikes the ground, respectively, are :
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Velocity just before collision }=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{gh}} \\
& \text { Velocity just after collision }=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g}\left(\frac{\mathrm{h}}{2}\right)} \\
& \therefore \Delta \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}(2 \mathrm{gh})-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mgh} \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mgh} \\
& \therefore \% \text { loss in energy } \\
& =\frac{\Delta \mathrm{KE}}{\mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{i}}} \times 100=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mgh}}{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mg} 2 \mathrm{~h}} \times 100=50 \%
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A body is moving unidirectionally under the influence of a constant power source. Its displacement in time $\mathrm{t}$ is proportional to :
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & P=\operatorname{constant} \Rightarrow \mathrm{FV}=\text { constant } \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{m} \frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dt}} \mathrm{V}=\text { constant } \\ & \int_0^{\mathrm{V}} \mathrm{VdV}=(\mathrm{C}) \int_0^{\mathrm{t}} \mathrm{dt} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{2}\right)=\mathrm{Ct} \\ & \mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{t}^{1 / 2} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{ds}}{\mathrm{dt}} \propto \mathrm{t}^{1 / 2} \\ & \int_0^{\mathrm{S}} \mathrm{ds}=\mathrm{K} \int_0^{\mathrm{t}} \mathrm{t}^{1 / 2} \mathrm{dt} \\ & \mathrm{S}=\mathrm{K} \times \frac{2}{3} \mathrm{t}^{3 / 2} \\ & \mathrm{~S} \propto \mathrm{t}^{3 / 2}\end{aligned}$
$\therefore$ displacement is proportional to $(\mathrm{t})^{3 / 2}$

questions.q: A bob of mass $m$ is suspended by a light string of length $L$. It is imparted a minimum horizontal velocity at the lowest point $A$ such that it just completes half circle reaching the top most position $B$. The ratio of kinetic energies $\dfrac{( K . E . {)}_{A}}{( K . E . {)}_{B}}$ is :
questions.solution:
The velocity given is minimum, just enough to complete verticle circle. At the top most point, tension of the string will be zero and gravitational force will provide the required centripetal force.

Therefore, 

$mg = \dfrac{m{\left({V}_{H}\right)}^{2}}{L} ⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left({V}_{H}\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}gL$

Apply energy conservation between point $A$ and $B$, we get

$\dfrac{1}{2}m{V}_{L}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{V}_{H}^{2} + mg ( 2L )$

$⇒ {V}_{L} = \sqrt{5gL}$

Also, ${V}_{H} = \sqrt{gL}$

Required ratio, $\dfrac{( K . E{)}_{A}}{( K . E{)}_{B}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}m ( \sqrt{5gL}{)}^{2}}{\dfrac{1}{2}m ( \sqrt{gL}{)}^{2}} = \dfrac{5}{1}$

questions.q: A body of mass $2kg$ begins to move under the action of a time dependent force given by $\overset{\to}{F} = \left(6t\overset{^}{i} + 6{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}\right)N$. The power developed by the force at the time $t$ is given by:
questions.solution:
Given: $\overset{\to}{F} = \left(6t\overset{^}{i} + 6{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}\right)N$

Now, $\overset{\to}{F} = m\overset{\to}{a} = \left(6t\overset{^}{i} + 6{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{a} = \overset{\to}{F}m = \left(3t\overset{^}{i} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}\right)$

Hence, velocity $\overset{\to}{v} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{t}\overset{\to}{a}dt = \dfrac{3{t}^{2}}{2}\overset{^}{i} + {t}^{3}\overset{^}{j}$

Required power, $P = \overset{\to}{F} . \overset{\to}{v} = \left(9{t}^{3} + 6{t}^{5}\right)W$

questions.q: A ball suspended by a thread swings in a vertical plane so that its magnitude of acceleration in the extreme position and lowest position are equal. The angle $( \theta )$ of thread deflection in the extreme position will be :
questions.solution:
At the lowermost point, there is no tangential force on the ball. Thus, there exists no tangential acceleration at the bottommost point, only the centripetal acceleration survives.

On the other hand, in the extreme position of the ball, there is no centripetal acceleration as the ball becomes momentarily at rest at that position. Here, only tangential acceleration survives.

Thus, with respect to the figure above, equating the kinetic energy at the bottommost point to the potential energy at the extreme point, we have
$\dfrac{1}{2}{mv}^{2} = mgl ( 1 - cos\theta ) ⇒ \dfrac{{v}^{2}}{l} = 2g ( 1 - cos\theta ) . . . \left(1\right)$

Now, the net acceleration $\left({a}_{t}\right)$ at the extreme point can be written as

${a}_{t} = gsin\theta . . . \left(2\right)$

According to the given problem, it follows that for the two positions of the ball,

${a}_{t} = \dfrac{{v}^{2}}{l} . . . \left(3\right)$

Equations (1), (2) and (3) imply that

$gsin\theta = 2g ( 1 - cos\theta ) ⇒ 2sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} = 4\sin^{2}\dfrac{\theta}{2} ⇒ tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ \theta = 2\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$
